desc:
Every node of a binary tree is the root of a subtree that consists of that node and all of its descendants. A subtree is single-valued if all of its nodes hold the same value. Return how many subtrees of the given tree are single-valued. Every leaf counts, and the empty tree has none.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 1, 1, 1, 2] the answer is 3: the two leaves holding 1 and the leaf holding 2. The left child of the root has children 1 and 2, and the root's subtree has two different values, so neither counts. For tree = [4, 4, 4, 4, 4, -1, 4] every one of the 6 subtrees is single-valued, so the answer is 6.
constraints: Every tree array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: A leaf is always single-valued. What do you need to know about the children of a node to decide about the node itself?
A node's subtree is single-valued exactly when each of its existing children roots a single-valued subtree and has the same value as the node.
Process nodes bottom-up (the reverse of level order works). Store one boolean per node, combine it from the children, and add one to a counter whenever the boolean is true.
editorial: Decide the question for every node, children first. For a node with value v the subtree is single-valued if and only if every existing child is the root of a single-valued subtree and its value equals v. Missing children impose no condition. The count is the number of nodes for which this holds.

Because children come after their parent in level order, walking the nodes from the last one to the first guarantees both children are decided before their parent, with no recursion needed (important for chain-shaped trees with 1,500 nodes). Each node is looked at once, so the algorithm is O(n) time and O(n) space.

A common mistake is to check only child.value == node.value without requiring the child's whole subtree to be single-valued: in [1, 1, 1, 1, 2] the left child equals the root's value but its subtree contains a 2.
